  • How many days should there be between periods?
Trying to Conceive

How many days should there be between periods?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

The gap between periods is not identical for everyone, and 28 days is only an average. Counting consistently and noticing changes in your own pattern is more useful than trying to make every month fit a textbook calendar.

Count from one period’s first day to the next

Cycle length is the number of days from the start of one period to the start of the next. It is not the number of days without bleeding between them. If a period begins on 1 May and the next begins on 29 May, the cycle was 28 days long. The second start begins a new count.

For a consistent record, mark the first day of established menstrual flow as day 1 and record any preceding spotting separately. Fertility clinics may give a more specific counting rule for tests or treatment. Also note when bleeding stops; cycle length and the duration of the period answer different questions.

Twenty-eight days is an average, not a requirement

Healthy patterns vary. NHS patient guidance commonly describes adult cycles of 21–35 days, while the US Office on Women’s Health uses 24–38 days. These are population guides with different definitions, not competing tests that make a 23-day or 36-day cycle automatically unhealthy.

Your usual pattern, age, contraception and accompanying symptoms matter. Some month-to-month variation is common, but a persistent change deserves discussion. Bleeding often lasts two to seven days and may be heavier at first, becoming lighter toward the end. A period does not have to last the same number of days every month to be worth recording accurately.

Why a cycle may become shorter

Ovulation and bleeding can shift with stress, anxiety, a recent illness such as flu, substantial weight change or changes in hormonal contraception. During perimenopause, cycles may initially become closer together and later more widely spaced. These are possible explanations, not a way to diagnose the cause from the calendar alone.

Sometimes what looks like an early period is bleeding between periods. Fibroids or a cycle without ovulation can produce bleeding that does not follow the expected pattern. Two periods in one calendar month do not necessarily mean an abnormally short cycle: a 28-day cycle beginning on the first day of a 31-day month can do this. Repeatedly short intervals, new spotting or symptoms warrant assessment rather than a fixed six-week wait.

Long gaps and the first years of periods

Cycles are often more variable after menstruation first begins. ACOG describes most adolescent cycles as 21–45 days, with increasing regularity over the following years. A gap of about 90 days deserves assessment even early on; it should not be dismissed simply because someone is young.

Counting only the number of periods in a year can hide long gaps. Four periods in a first year or nine in an adult year is not, by itself, proof that the pattern is healthy. Seek advice if periods have not begun by age 15, or within three years of breast development. Earlier review is appropriate when there are other concerns, such as significant food restriction, marked hair growth or pain.

Why adult periods may become further apart

Stress, inadequate energy intake, demanding exercise, weight changes, breastfeeding, hormonal contraception and the menopause transition can delay or suppress ovulation. Pregnancy must also be considered when possible. Some contraceptive methods deliberately reduce or stop bleeding, so spontaneous-cycle ranges may not apply to their bleeding patterns.

Hormone conditions can contribute. PMOS, formerly called PCOS, may cause irregular cycles alongside acne, increased facial or body hair or other symptoms. Primary ovarian insufficiency affects ovarian function before age 40 and can cause missed periods or menopausal symptoms. Thyroid problems and other illnesses are also possible. None can be confirmed from the length of a cycle or one symptom; testing follows the individual history.

Menstruation is one part of an overlapping cycle

The menstrual cycle is often described in four parts: menstruation, the follicular phase, ovulation and the luteal phase. These are useful explanations rather than four separate calendar blocks. Menstruation occurs during the early follicular phase, while the ovaries are already preparing for the next potential ovulation.

When pregnancy has not developed, falling hormone levels allow the uterine lining to shed. Menstrual fluid contains blood, lining tissue and secretions. The amount and colour change through a period, and darker blood near the end can reflect slower passage. Appearance alone cannot reveal hormone levels, diagnose infertility or reliably distinguish a period from every other cause of bleeding.

The follicular phase prepares an egg

Hormone signals between the brain and ovaries coordinate the cycle. Follicle-stimulating hormone, or FSH, supports a group of follicles in the ovary. Each follicle contains an immature egg; usually one becomes dominant. There is no fixed number of developing follicles that every person should have in every cycle.

The developing follicle produces oestrogen, helping the uterine lining grow. The length of this phase can vary, which is one reason ovulation and the next period may come earlier or later than expected. An app can estimate the pattern from past dates, but it cannot see follicle development or prove that an egg has been released.

Ovulation does not always happen on day 14

A rise in luteinising hormone, or LH, helps trigger release of the egg from the dominant follicle. It can then enter a fallopian tube, where fertilisation may occur. An egg is usually available for fertilisation for roughly 12–24 hours, but sperm present before ovulation can also lead to pregnancy.

Day 14 is a simplified example for a 28-day cycle, not a universal appointment. Ovulation may shift even when previous cycles looked regular. A calendar prediction therefore does not confirm a fertile or infertile day. If an egg is not fertilised, it breaks down; it is microscopic and is not a visible object that you should expect to identify in menstrual blood.

The luteal phase supports the uterine lining

After ovulation, the emptied follicle becomes the corpus luteum and produces progesterone. This helps prepare the uterine lining for a possible pregnancy. If pregnancy does not develop, the corpus luteum’s activity declines, progesterone and oestrogen fall, and another period begins.

This phase commonly lasts around two weeks, with individual variation. Public and specialist references describe somewhat different ranges, so it is better not to assign everyone an exact 12-, 14- or 15-day phase. A short-looking interval on an app does not diagnose progesterone deficiency. ASRM notes that no available test reliably distinguishes a luteal-phase defect in fertile and infertile people in ordinary clinical practice.

Track the details that help a clinician

A paper calendar or an app can record start and end dates, spotting, unexpectedly heavy days and clots. Note how often products become saturated, leakage and whether bleeding disrupts sleep or normal activities. Product counts are useful context but do not measure blood loss precisely because absorbency and changing habits differ.

Record pain severity and location, whether it occurs outside the period, and bleeding after sex. Mood changes, breast symptoms and headaches may reveal a repeating pattern, but tracking alone does not prove PMS or exclude another condition. Include medicine, contraception, illness, exercise or feeding changes. Use a method you can maintain without pressure to log every sensation, and consider an app’s privacy settings.

Testing and symptoms that need attention

If pregnancy is possible, test from the first missed period day. When the due date is unclear, test at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex. Repeat an early negative after a few days if needed. A blood test is sometimes useful, but everyone with a delayed period does not automatically need one.

Arrange assessment for three missed periods, persistently unusual cycle intervals, bleeding lasting over a week, recurrent large clots or bleeding between periods or after sex. Do not wait for these thresholds if pain, fatigue or other symptoms are significant. Soaking a pad or tampon every hour repeatedly needs urgent advice; heavy bleeding with faintness, breathlessness or chest pain is an emergency.

When pregnancy is possible, unusual bleeding with one-sided pelvic pain or shoulder-tip pain needs prompt assessment. Severe abdominal pain, fainting or collapse requires emergency care even without a positive home test. Bleeding after menopause also needs medical assessment.

What happens at a review

A clinician will usually start with your dates, symptoms, pregnancy possibility, medicines and life stage. Depending on the findings, a pregnancy test, blood count, thyroid or other hormone tests, examination or ultrasound may help. Not everyone needs all these tests, and an ultrasound alone does not explain every irregular cycle.

Treatment addresses the cause and your priorities, including comfort, bleeding control, bone or uterine health and pregnancy plans. It may involve support with nutrition or stress, adjusting contraception or treating a specific condition. Simply producing a scheduled bleed is not the same as proving that spontaneous ovulation has returned. Agree when to review the pattern again and which changes should prompt earlier contact.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Cycle reference ranges vary by age, definition and use of hormonal contraception.

Calendar estimates do not confirm ovulation, diagnose a hormone condition or establish contraception-safe days.

How BeMama can help

Record dates, symptoms and relevant changes in a simple format you can bring to an appointment.

When to seek help

Seek urgent advice for repeated hourly product saturation. Heavy bleeding with faintness, breathlessness or chest pain, or severe pain and collapse when pregnancy is possible, needs emergency care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Count from the first day of one period to the first day of the next.
  • A cycle does not need to be exactly 28 days.
  • Adolescent and contraceptive bleeding patterns need their own context.
  • The follicular phase, ovulation and luteal phase cannot be assigned fixed dates for everyone.
  • Persistent changes, significant bleeding or pregnancy-related symptoms deserve timely assessment.

Frequently asked questions

Do I count the days after bleeding stops?

No. Cycle length runs from the start of one period to the start of the next. Record the bleeding duration separately so you do not confuse a 28-day cycle with 28 days without bleeding.

Is a 36-day cycle definitely abnormal?

Not automatically. Adult reference ranges differ, and an occasional longer cycle can occur. Your established pattern, age, symptoms and pregnancy possibility help determine whether it needs assessment.

Can two periods in a calendar month be normal?

Yes. A cycle can begin twice within a long calendar month without being unusually short. Count the actual days between starts and report unexpected spotting or a persistent change.

Is it enough to have four periods in the first year?

An annual total is not a reliable health check. Adolescents can have variable cycles, but a gap of about 90 days warrants review even early in menstrual life.

Does ovulation always occur on day 14?

No. That is a simplified example, and timing can change between cycles. An app’s estimate cannot confirm ovulation or identify days when pregnancy is impossible.

Will I see the unfertilised egg in my period?

No. The egg is microscopic and breaks down if it is not fertilised. Visible clots or tissue in menstrual flow are not an identifiable egg.

Does a short luteal phase on an app mean I need progesterone?

No. Predicted dates may be inaccurate, and timing alone does not diagnose a treatable deficiency. Discuss persistent concerns or fertility difficulties before taking hormones.

When should I test if my cycles are unpredictable?

If you cannot identify a due date, test at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex. Repeat an early negative if pregnancy remains possible and seek advice if periods remain absent.

Can contraception make cycle-length rules less useful?

Yes. Hormonal methods can cause withdrawal bleeding, spotting or no bleeding at all. Follow advice for the particular method and assess new symptoms or missed doses separately.

Must I wait six weeks before asking about a change?

No. There is no universal waiting rule. Severe symptoms, pregnancy concerns or heavy bleeding need earlier help; ongoing changes can be discussed even before a formal threshold is reached.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
